findings.claim: Juliet, just before drinking the Friar's potion, imagines “my Romeo's body dead in the street.”
findings.truth: Fabricated quotation. Before the potion (4.3) Juliet imagines Tybalt's ghost “seeking out Romeo”; her vision of Romeo dead comes at the dawn parting (3.5): “Methinks I see thee, now thou art so low, / As one dead in the bottom of a tomb.” Replaced with the real line. The dependent flashcard (“that Juliet later echoes”) was trimmed too.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg text lines 3544-3546 (3.5) and 4247-4249 (4.3); no line matching “dead in the street” exists in the play.

findings.claim: Juliet is described by Paris as a “green” fruit to be bought through Capulet.
findings.truth: The ripeness image is Capulet's, not Paris's: “Ere we may think her ripe to be a bride” (1.2). Paris only answers “Younger than she are happy mothers made.” Capulet also tells Paris that Juliet's consent is part of his own.

findings.claim: Their first conversation is a shared sonnet (Act 1 Scene 5), with Juliet taking four of the fourteen lines.
findings.truth: Juliet takes six of the fourteen lines: the second quatrain (four lines) plus two single lines in the third quatrain.

findings.claim: All six lesson 1 ladders use “Mastering / Secure / Developing / Emerging” with no mark ranges.
findings.truth: Malformed ladder names and no mark bands. Rescaled to the house five-band ladder over the real 40-mark total: Top (33-40) / Upper-mid (25-32) / Mid (17-24) / Lower-mid (9-16) / Low (1-8). The lessons 2-8 six-band 40-mark ladders are correct and were left alone.
findings.evidence: Spec p.16: Component 02 is 2 hours, 80 marks, 40 marks per section.

findings.claim: The Prince: “If ever you disturb our streets again, / Your lives shall pay the forfeit of your peace.”
findings.truth: The line reads “Your lives shall pay the forfeit of the peace.” Fixed in the lesson body and in the flashcard answer.

findings.claim: Section heading “The Secret Marriage (Act 2, Scene 6)” over a paragraph quoting “this alliance may so happy prove”.
findings.truth: That line is Act 2 Scene 3, where the Friar agrees to the marriage. Only “These violent delights have violent ends” is 2.6. Heading widened to “Act 2, Scenes 3 and 6”.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg text line 1990 (2.3, scene block 1857-2000) and line 2515 (2.6).

findings.claim: The literal spec code “OCR J352” appears 12 times across lessons 2-8 (L2 exam tip, L3 body, L4 body + exam tip, L5 exam tip, L6 description + exam tip, L7 exam tip, L8 description + conclusion + exam tip + a practice question + a knowledge check), plus one “the OCR extract question” in the L3 exam tip.
findings.truth: Banned string in lesson fields. Every instance rewritten in the house vocabulary; no exam fact changed by these edits.

findings.claim: Lesson 2 description is 101 characters; lesson 7 description is 103 characters.
findings.truth: The validator wants the description under 100 characters. Both trimmed without losing content.

findings.claim: 21 practice questions across lessons 2-8 are typed “4 marks — Quote Analysis” while their ladders run Top band (7-8) down to Lower band (1-2).
findings.truth: The ladder is an 8-mark ladder, so the label contradicts it. Relabelled “8 marks — Quote Analysis”, matching the fix made in the three earlier OCR Shakespeare units.
findings.evidence: The marks string on each question.

findings.claim: “Her death takes only four lines — compared to Romeo's elaborate 20-line speech” (repeated in the L5 mark ladder, the L6 body and an L6 flashcard).
findings.truth: Romeo's final speech runs about thirty lines (“How oft when men are at the point of death” to “Thus with a kiss I die”); Juliet's dying speech runs about ten. The contrast the lesson draws is sound; only the counts were wrong.

findings.claim: She “hangs upon the cheek of night / Like a rich jewel in an Ethiope's ear” (also on a flashcard).
findings.truth: The line reads “As a rich jewel in an Ethiop's ear” (1.5). Both places corrected; it is still a simile.

findings.claim: Flashcard: “Quote Romeo's oxymoron personifying Death as Juliet's lover.”
findings.truth: “That unsubstantial Death is amorous” is personification, not an oxymoron; the lesson body already calls it personification. Naming the wrong technique in an answer costs analysis marks.
An AO code immediately followed by a full stop trips the house validator's spec-code pattern. Reworded to “strong AO2 evidence.”

findings.claim: “you have approximately 45 minutes. Spend 5 minutes planning, 35 minutes writing... Never leave the SPaG check to chance — it is worth up to 4 marks.” (the 5/35/5 split is repeated in a mark ladder).
findings.truth: The poetry and Shakespeare paper is 2 hours for 80 marks, 40 marks for each of the two sections, so the Shakespeare question is worth about an hour, not 45 minutes. Retimed to 10 / 45 / 5. The spec carries no mark grids, so “up to 4 marks” for SPaG is an invented number; replaced with a statement naming the objective without a figure.
findings.evidence: Spec p.16 (Component 02: closed text, 2 hours, 80 marks, 40 + 40) and p.17-18 (AO weighting table; AO4 assessed in Section B, no mark grid given).

findings.claim: Flashcard answer “'Hang, beg, starve, die in the streets.'”
findings.truth: A bare comma list is rejected as an enumeration. The quotation moved into the question and the answer now states what Capulet means.
findings.evidence: CHECK_PROMPT.md validator limits; Gutenberg text line 3780 (3.5).

findings.claim: Three quotations differ from the Gutenberg (Globe-based) text: “Romeo, I come! This do I drink to thee” (L4 flashcard; Gutenberg reads “Romeo, Romeo, Romeo, here's drink! I drink to thee”), “there rust, and let me die” (L5; Gutenberg “There rest”), and “Do with their death bury their parents' strife” (L1 extract; Gutenberg “Doth”).
findings.truth: These are early-quarto / folio variants, not errors. The lesson readings are the ones printed in the school editions students use. Left as they are.

findings.claim: The practice bank mixes 40-mark essay questions with 21 short 8-mark “Quote Analysis” items.
findings.truth: The real Section B is a single 40-mark extended response from a choice of two, so the short items are house practice, not board format. They are useful, and the labels now match their own ladders, but the unit never says the short items are exam questions.

findings.claim: Lesson titles “Acts 1-2”, “Acts 2-3”, “Acts 3-4”, “Acts 4-5” overlap and do not match the content exactly (lesson 3 covers 1.4 and all of Act 3; lesson 5 covers Act 5 only).
findings.truth: Cosmetic overlap in the unit map, not a factual error. Titles are not editable through _edits.json.

summary: Two HIGH errors: lesson 1 invents a Juliet quotation (“my Romeo's body dead in the street”) that is nowhere in the play, and lesson 8 tells students the Shakespeare question is worth 45 minutes when the paper gives 2 hours for two 40-mark sections, so it is about an hour. Every other quotation in all eight lessons checks out against the Gutenberg text for wording, speaker and act.scene apart from three small misquotations (“forfeit of your peace”, “Like a rich jewel”, and a Paris/Capulet misattribution) and two wrong line counts for the death speeches; the rest of the yield is the banned board-code phrasing in 13 places (“OCR J352” 12 times), 21 mark-label mismatches, one malformed lesson 1 ladder set and validator-limit trims.
